cards.title: Constant-additive real-weighted APSP in near-quadratic time when ω=2
cards.formal: Assuming matrix multiplication exponent ω=2, is there an algorithm and absolute constants C>0 and a≥0 that, on every n-vertex undirected graph with real edge weights in [0,1], outputs all-pairs distance estimates D̂ satisfying dist_G(u,v)≤D̂(u,v)≤dist_G(u,v)+C for every connected pair, in O(n²(log(n+1))^a) time? For disconnected pairs the output must be ∞. C is independent of n, the graph and the edge weights; the source asks whether even some large constant additive error is achievable, not necessarily every prescribed ε>0. The exact real-arithmetic and randomized-time conventions remain to be specified.
cards.why: Would determine whether a constant amount of additive error removes the gap between real-weighted all-pairs distances and the quadratic size of their output, even under the most optimistic matrix exponent.
cards.status_note: Read the complete ESA 2021 paper, the full author preprint of the SODA 2026 unweighted follow-up, and current author/publication records. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no solution to the stated real-weighted target. Machine and exact exponent conventions remain unfinished.

progress.text: The source gives exponent (3+ω²)/(ω+1) for arbitrary fixed additive accuracy and poses the near-quadratic constant-error question.

importance.reason: Tests a substantial barrier between real-weighted shortest paths and near-output-linear computation under constant additive error. Existing score retained.

sentences: The graph is undirected and its arbitrary real edge weights lie between zero and one.
The algorithm must output every distance with no underestimation and only a constant additive error.
The target time is n² up to polylogarithmic factors under the source’s ω=2 hypothesis.
The known source bound has exponent 7/3 when evaluated at ω=2, and recent unweighted improvements do not settle this real-weighted problem.
The precise real-arithmetic machine, randomization and exponent-attainment conventions remain to be fixed.

cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E), with V=[n] and an explicit real weight w(e)∈[0,1] for every edge. dist_G(u,v) is the minimum sum of edge weights on a path from u to v, equals zero when u=v, and is ∞ if no path exists. Zero-weight edges are allowed and negative weights are not. All n² estimates are output explicitly; a data structure answering only selected distance queries is a different output requirement. The inequalities forbid underestimation, and the tolerance C is additive in the normalized edge-weight scale rather than a factor times dist_G(u,v). For arbitrary bounded nonnegative weights the corresponding guarantee is C times the maximum edge weight after rescaling. Õ(n²) here denotes n² times a fixed polylogarithmic factor, not an unspecified n^{o(1)} factor. The matrix multiplication exponent is ordinarily the infimum of τ for which two s×s matrices can be multiplied using O(s^τ) arithmetic operations; ω=2 as an infimum supplies exponents arbitrarily close to two, but does not by itself assert an O(s² polylog s) algorithm. The paper measures arithmetic-algorithm running time on real-valued input, rather than Turing bit complexity for arbitrary finite-precision weights. Its exact primitive operations, uniformity and randomization conventions must be recorded before claiming a fully self-contained machine-level target.
cards.answer_criterion: After fixing the source-compatible computational and matrix-exponent conventions, prove or refute existence of the stated algorithm for some absolute additive constant C. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real weights in [0,1] and all vertex pairs in the stated time. Unweighted-only results, multiplicative approximation, error growing with n, or a larger subpolynomial overhead do not by themselves meet the displayed target.

context_blocks.title: Small absolute error remains demanding on long paths
context_blocks.text: A constant multiplicative approximation may incur error proportional to the entire path length. The additive guarantee here permits only a constant number of maximum-edge-weight units of error, even when the shortest path uses many edges.

context_blocks.title: The source leaves a substantial gap at exponent two
context_blocks.text: The paper’s bound has exponent (3+ω²)/(ω+1), yielding 7/3 when ω is set to two, for any fixed positive additive tolerance. Its first final remark asks whether a near-quadratic bound could hold even if the allowed constant error is much larger.

context_blocks.title: Recent unweighted improvements do not settle real weights
context_blocks.text: The SODA 2026 work improves algorithms with additive errors two, four and six on unweighted undirected graphs. Its complete statements keep that unweighted assumption. These results therefore do not supply the arbitrary-real-weight guarantee required by the source question.

context_blocks.title: The matrix hypothesis and precision need care
context_blocks.text: An exponent defined as an infimum can differ from an attained bound with only logarithmic overhead. This distinction matters because the question explicitly requests Õ(n²). The card preserves that requested precision instead of silently replacing it by n^{2+o(1)}.

context_blocks.title: Remaining specification
context_blocks.text: The statement’s asymptotic target is recoverable, but a complete benchmark must fix the exact unit-cost real-arithmetic operations and the permitted randomness/error and worst-case versus expected running time. The source does not give a full machine definition. It should also confirm whether its use of ω=2 denotes the infimum-exponent hypothesis alone or an attained Õ(n²) matrix-multiplication algorithm; these hypotheses are not identical, so the latter is not substituted silently.

cards.context:
A constant multiplicative approximation may incur error proportional to the entire path length. The additive guarantee here permits only a constant number of maximum-edge-weight units of error, even when the shortest path uses many edges.

The paper’s bound has exponent (3+ω²)/(ω+1), yielding 7/3 when ω is set to two, for any fixed positive additive tolerance. Its first final remark asks whether a near-quadratic bound could hold even if the allowed constant error is much larger.

The SODA 2026 work improves algorithms with additive errors two, four and six on unweighted undirected graphs. Its complete statements keep that unweighted assumption. These results therefore do not supply the arbitrary-real-weight guarantee required by the source question.

An exponent defined as an infimum can differ from an attained bound with only logarithmic overhead. This distinction matters because the question explicitly requests Õ(n²). The card preserves that requested precision instead of silently replacing it by n^{2+o(1)}.

The statement’s asymptotic target is recoverable, but a complete benchmark must fix the exact unit-cost real-arithmetic operations and the permitted randomness/error and worst-case versus expected running time. The source does not give a full machine definition. It should also confirm whether its use of ω=2 denotes the infimum-exponent hypothesis alone or an attained Õ(n²) matrix-multiplication algorithm; these hypotheses are not identical, so the latter is not substituted silently.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
